title: First with the idea, second with the money
lede: Much of what a fast-food counter now offers appeared at Burger Chef early: the combination meal, the double-decker burger, the children’s meal in a box, the condiment bar. None of it was protected well enough, or backed heavily enough, to matter.

blocks.title: Firsts, with their dates

items.text: The “Triple Threat” or “Triple Treat”: burger, fries and a drink sold together, which Time calls the first combo meal.[^4][^7]
The Big Shef, a double-decker with cheese, lettuce and sauce, two or three years before the Big Mac.[^7][^8]
The Funmeal, a boxed children’s meal with games and a small toy or record. The Happy Meal followed in 1979.[^17][^20]
Star Wars Funmeal trays in 1978, an early film tie-in for a children’s meal.[^17][^19]

blocks.source: Time[^4], Indianapolis Star[^7], Indiana Historical Bureau[^8], Mental Floss[^17], Griffin Museum of Science and Industry[^19]. “First” claims are those of the cited sources.

blocks.title: The children’s meal
blocks.caption: Original illustration of a fold-up meal tray of the kind the Funmeal introduced. Not a reproduction of any Burger Chef packaging.
blocks.body: The box was the product. It folded into a tray, carried puzzles and stories, and gave children a reason to ask for one chain over another. Mental Floss reports that McDonald’s executives knew of the Funmeal when they commissioned the Happy Meal.[^17]

blocks.title: The Happy Meal dispute
blocks.body: The Indianapolis Star records that Burger Chef sued McDonald’s after the Happy Meal appeared in 1979, and that a 1981 suit against Burger King over a “Fun School Meal” was settled out of court when Burger King acknowledged the Funmeal trademark.[^7] A 2025 essay says the McDonald’s case was dismissed because the idea of a bundled children’s meal was too broad to protect.[^18] We did not find the court record. Treat the outcome, and any damages figure quoted elsewhere, as **unverified**.

blocks.title: Advertising
blocks.body: McCann Erickson won the account in 1968, with billings of $2.5 million, and resigned it in 1971, when Ogilvy & Mather took over.[^4] The animated mascots Burger Chef and Jeff fronted the children’s advertising through the 1970s.[^6][^8] The total advertising budget in later years is unknown.
